title: The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Criticism
author: Alexander Pope
setting: Belinda’s bedroom, the Thames and Hampton Court in Queen Anne’s reign, with a descent to the Cave of Spleen
lengthNote: The Rape of the Lock runs to 794 lines in five cantos and An Essay on Criticism to 744 lines in three parts, almost all in rhyming couplets of ten syllables
openingLine: What dire offence from am'rous causes springs,
summary: Two poems by the young Alexander Pope. The Rape of the Lock began with a real quarrel: in 1711 Lord Petre cut off a lock of Arabella Fermor’s hair, and a friend of both Catholic families asked Pope for a poem that might laugh them out of it. Pope told the story as an epic in miniature. Belinda wakes from a dream sent by her guardian sylph, arms herself at her dressing table, sails up the Thames to Hampton Court and wins a game of ombre before the Baron cuts the curl with scissors lent by Clarissa. A gnome brings sighs and tears from the Cave of Spleen, the beaux and belles fight a battle with fans and snuff, and the lock rises to the stars. An Essay on Criticism, published in 1711, argues in verse about how poetry should be judged: follow Nature, learn from the ancients, beware of pride and of a little learning, and be a critic who is learned, candid and humane. Many of its lines have become proverbs.
referenceStyle: canto and line for The Rape of the Lock (Canto III, 21–22) and line for An Essay on Criticism (Essay, 215), following the line numbers of Parrott’s 1906 edition

sourceText.label: The Rape of the Lock and Other Poems, ed. Thomas Marc Parrott (Boston: Ginn, 1906), Project Gutenberg eBook 9800
sourceText.note: Parrott prints both poems in their final forms, from A. W. Ward’s Globe edition, and adds the two-canto first version of The Rape of the Lock (1712) as an appendix. Quotations follow his text, with its elisions (ev’ry, th’) and capitals, and his line numbers.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: An Essay on Criticism appeared without Pope’s name on 15 May 1711. The Rape of the Lock first appeared, in two cantos, in Lintot’s Miscellany in May 1712.

atAGlance.label: Rewritten
atAGlance.note: In 1714 Pope enlarged the Rape to five cantos and added the sylphs and gnomes. Clarissa’s speech followed in 1717.

atAGlance.label: The real quarrel
atAGlance.note: In 1711 Robert, Lord Petre, then about twenty, cut a lock of hair from Arabella Fermor, and a friend of both families asked Pope for a poem to end the quarrel.

atAGlance.label: Verse
atAGlance.note: Rhyming pairs of ten-syllable lines, usually closed, so that each couplet completes a thought.

structure.label: Canto I
structure.title: The dream and the dressing table
structure.summary: The poet announces his subject, the dire offence that rose from amorous causes, and asks the Muse what could make a well-bred lord assault a gentle belle. At noon Belinda is still asleep, and her guardian sylph, Ariel, sends her a dream. A glittering youth tells her that thousands of spirits of the air protect her, explains that the souls of dead coquettes become sylphs and those of prudes become gnomes, and warns her of some dreadful event that day. Her lapdog Shock licks her awake, and a love letter drives the vision from her head. At her dressing table she worships her own reflection while the sylphs help her maid, Betty, to arm her for the day.

scenes.title: The invocation
scenes.summary: Mighty contests from trivial things, and a question for the Muse.

scenes.title: Ariel’s warning
scenes.summary: A morning dream of sylphs, gnomes and the afterlife of coquettes, ending with a warning against Man.

scenes.title: The billet-doux
scenes.summary: Shock wakes his mistress, and a love letter chases the dream away.

scenes.title: The toilet
scenes.summary: Cosmetic powers worshipped at a dressing table laid with the offerings of the world.

structure.label: Canto II
structure.title: The Thames and the Baron’s altar
structure.summary: Belinda sails up the Thames, as bright as the sun and as impartial with her smiles, wearing a cross that Jews might kiss and infidels adore. Two curls hang down her neck. The Baron has resolved to have one of them, by force or by fraud, and before dawn he built an altar of twelve French romances and burned old love letters on it; the gods granted half his prayer. On the boat Ariel gathers the sylphs, reminds them of their duties to the fair, gives each a charge, and sets fifty of them to guard the petticoat, threatening any deserter with pins, pomatum and the chocolate mill.

scenes.title: Belinda on the river
scenes.summary: The rival of the sun, her cross and her two locks.

scenes.title: The Baron’s prayer
scenes.summary: An altar of French romances and a prayer half granted.

scenes.title: Ariel’s charge
scenes.summary: Sylphs in the rigging, the duties of the airy kind, and a guard for the petticoat.

structure.label: Canto III
structure.title: Hampton Court, ombre and the scissors
structure.summary: At Hampton Court, where Queen Anne sometimes takes counsel and sometimes tea, the company gossips while judges hurry their sentences so that the jury can dine. Belinda challenges two knights to ombre, the card game is fought as an epic battle, and she wins the last trick. Coffee is served, and its fumes send new stratagems to the Baron’s brain. Clarissa hands him a pair of scissors. The sylphs blow back the hair and tug at Belinda’s earring, but Ariel finds an earthly lover in her thoughts and gives up his guard; a sylph who gets in the way is cut in two, and the lock is severed. Belinda screams, and the Baron boasts that his honour will live as long as ladies pay visits.

scenes.title: The court
scenes.summary: Heroes and nymphs at Hampton Court, gossip, snuff and the hungry judges.

scenes.title: Ombre
scenes.summary: Kings, queens and knaves in battle on the velvet plain.

scenes.title: The lock is cut
scenes.summary: Coffee, Clarissa’s scissors, Ariel’s retreat and a scream.

scenes.title: The victor’s boast
scenes.summary: Wreaths of triumph and the conquering force of steel.

structure.label: Canto IV
structure.title: The Cave of Spleen
structure.summary: No captive king or ageing beauty ever felt such rage as Belinda. The gnome Umbriel flies down to the Cave of Spleen, a gloomy grotto where the goddess sighs on her bed between Pain and Megrim, attended by Ill-nature and Affectation, among living teapots, a sighing jar and a talking goose-pie. He asks her to touch Belinda with chagrin, and she gives him a bag of sighs, sobs and quarrels and a vial of fears, sorrows and tears. He empties the bag over Belinda and her friend Thalestris. Thalestris sends her beau, Sir Plume, to demand the lock; he swears at the Baron, who will not give it up. Umbriel breaks the vial, and Belinda weeps and wishes she had never seen Hampton Court.

scenes.title: Belinda’s rage
scenes.summary: Rage, resentment and despair for a ravished hair.

scenes.title: Umbriel’s descent
scenes.summary: The grotto of Spleen, her handmaids, her phantoms, the bag and the vial.

scenes.title: Thalestris and Sir Plume
scenes.summary: A call to defend Belinda’s honour, and a beau’s oaths.

scenes.title: Belinda’s lament
scenes.summary: Tears, remembered omens, and the sister-lock that still hangs.

structure.label: Canto V
structure.title: The battle and the new star
structure.summary: The Baron is unmoved. Clarissa waves her fan for silence and makes a speech that Pope added in 1717: beauty fades and locks turn grey, so good sense and good humour must keep what beauty wins. No one applauds, and Thalestris calls her a prude. The beaux and belles fall on each other in a battle of frowns, fans and snuff, with Umbriel watching from a sconce, and Jove weighs the men’s wits against the lady’s hair. Belinda throws snuff at the Baron’s nose, draws a bodkin that has come down through her family, and demands the lock, but it has vanished. The Muse saw it rise into the heavens as a new star, which will keep Belinda’s name alive when her own beauty is dust.

scenes.title: Clarissa’s speech
scenes.summary: Good sense and good humour, added in 1717.

scenes.title: The battle
scenes.summary: Beaux die in metaphor and in song, and Jove weighs wits against hair.

scenes.title: Snuff and the bodkin
scenes.summary: Belinda’s charge, the Baron’s fall, and a lock nowhere to be found.

scenes.title: The new star
scenes.summary: The lunar sphere, the Muse’s sight, and a trail of hair across the sky.

structure.label: An Essay on Criticism, Part I
structure.title: Nature, the rules and the ancients
structure.summary: The Essay begins by weighing bad critics against bad writers and finds the critics more dangerous. True taste is as rare as true genius, though most people have the seeds of judgement until false learning spoils them. A critic must know the limits of his own powers and follow Nature, the universal standard. The rules of the ancients are Nature methodised, discovered in the practice of Homer and the other great poets, and Virgil found that Nature and Homer were the same. Some beauties lie beyond any rule, and great poets may take a lucky licence. Part I ends with praise of the ancient bards and a prayer that some spark of their fire may inspire the last and meanest of their sons.

scenes.title: Critics and writers
scenes.summary: Judging ill is worse than writing ill; taste, false learning and the limits of wit.

scenes.title: Follow Nature
scenes.summary: Nature as the standard, the rules as Nature methodised, and Virgil’s discovery.

scenes.title: Licence and the ancients
scenes.summary: A grace beyond the reach of art, and a hymn to the ancient bards.

structure.label: An Essay on Criticism, Part II
structure.title: Why critics judge badly
structure.summary: Part II sets out the causes that hinder true judgement. The first is pride, the second a little learning. Critics judge by parts, not by the whole, and fix on conceits, on language or on the smoothness of the metre; here Pope makes his lines imitate the faults and virtues they describe, so that the sound seems an echo to the sense. Other critics are too hard to please or too quick to admire, partial to the ancients or the moderns, swayed by fashion, by a lord’s name, by party or by envy. Towards the end comes a plea for good nature, to err is human, to forgive, divine, and a direction for the critic’s anger: obscenity and blasphemy deserve it.

scenes.title: Pride and a little learning
scenes.summary: The never-failing voice of fools, and the Alps of learning.

scenes.title: Parts and the whole
scenes.summary: Conceit, language and numbers, and the sound that echoes the sense.

scenes.title: Extremes, fashion and envy
scenes.summary: Too hard to please, too apt to admire, following the town, the lord and the party.

scenes.title: Good nature
scenes.summary: To err is human, and the crimes that deserve a critic’s rage.

structure.label: An Essay on Criticism, Part III
structure.title: The good critic
structure.summary: Part III turns from judgement to manners. The critic should be candid and modest, own his errors, give advice without arrogance, and know when to stay silent, since some bad poets cannot be mended and some critics, like the bookful blockhead, will talk you dead even at the altar. Pope then asks where the ideal critic is to be found, and answers with a history of criticism: Aristotle, Horace, Dionysius, Petronius, Quintilian and Longinus; the fall of learning with Rome and its revival under Erasmus and Pope Leo X; Vida in Italy, Boileau in France, and in England Roscommon and William Walsh, the friend who had taught Pope’s Muse to sing. The Essay closes with a portrait of that Muse.

scenes.title: The critic’s manners
scenes.summary: Candour, good breeding, silence, and the bookful blockhead.

scenes.title: The ideal critic
scenes.summary: Where is the man? Aristotle, Horace, Quintilian and Longinus.

scenes.title: Decline and revival
scenes.summary: Monks and Goths, Erasmus, Vida, Boileau, Roscommon and Walsh.

characters.name: Belinda
characters.role: The belle whose lock is cut
characters.summary: Admired by every eye on the Thames, Belinda is a young beauty of Queen Anne’s London, with a sparkling cross on her breast and two curls on her neck. At her dressing table she is the chief priestess, and the goddess she worships is her own reflection. She wins at ombre, loses the lock, rages, weeps, throws snuff in the Baron’s face and demands her hair back. In his dedication Pope told Arabella Fermor that Belinda resembled her in nothing but beauty.
characters.clue: She wakes at noon, worships her reflection, wins at ombre, and throws a charge of snuff at the man who cut her hair.

characters.name: The Baron
characters.role: The lord who cuts the lock
characters.summary: An adventurous young peer who sees Belinda’s curls, wants one, and prays for it at dawn at an altar made of French romances. He plays ombre against her and nearly wins, then, with coffee in his brain and Clarissa’s scissors in his hand, cuts the lock and claims it as a conqueror. He refuses Sir Plume, swears by the lock to wear it for ever, and is brought down by a pinch of snuff. Pope based him on Robert, Lord Petre, who was about twenty when he cut a lock of Arabella Fermor’s hair in 1711.
characters.clue: Before dawn he burns old love letters on an altar of twelve French romances, and he ends the poem sneezing under a charge of snuff.

characters.name: Ariel
characters.summary: The chief of the sylphs, the airy spirits Pope borrowed from the Rosicrucian lore of Le Comte de Gabalis. He sends Belinda her morning dream, warns her to beware of man, commands the sylphs from the mast of her boat, and perches on a matadore at ombre. His power lasts only while she rejects mankind, and when he finds an earthly lover in her heart he withdraws with a sigh. After the lock is cut he flies from her weeping.
characters.clue: From a gilded mast he hands each spirit its charge: the fan, the earrings, the watch, the favourite curl, and the lapdog, which he keeps for himself.

characters.name: Umbriel
characters.role: The gnome who brings Belinda sorrow
characters.summary: Umbriel is a dusky, melancholy sprite, one of the gnomes into which the souls of prudes sink after death. When the sylphs withdraw he flies down to the Cave of Spleen with a sprig of spleenwort, as Aeneas carried the golden bough into the underworld, flatters its goddess, and brings back a bag of sighs and quarrels and a vial of tears, which he empties over Belinda and Thalestris. He watches the battle in triumph from a sconce.
characters.clue: With a sprig of spleenwort in his hand he walks past living teapots to ask a favour of a sighing goddess.

characters.name: Clarissa
characters.role: The lady who lends the scissors and speaks for good sense
characters.summary: A lady of the party who draws a two-edged weapon from her case and hands it to the Baron, as ladies in romance arm their knights. In the fifth canto, in a speech Pope added in 1717 to make the moral of the poem clearer, she tells Belinda that beauty fades and that good sense and good humour must keep what beauty wins. Her speech parodies Sarpedon’s speech to Glaucus in the Iliad. No one applauds, and in the battle Sir Plume pulls her down.
characters.clue: She hands over a two-edged weapon from her shining case, and later waves her fan to preach good humour to a room that will not clap.

characters.name: Thalestris
characters.summary: Named after a queen of the Amazons, she holds Belinda in her arms, fans her anger, and cries out that Belinda’s honour will be lost if the Baron keeps the lock. She sends her beau, Sir Plume, to demand it back, calls Clarissa a prude, raises the call to arms, and scatters death around her with her eyes in the battle. She is said to have been drawn from a Mrs Morley, sister of Sir George Brown.
characters.clue: Named after an Amazon queen, she cries O wretched maid!, sends her beau to demand the hair, and calls a sober speaker a prude.

characters.name: Sir Plume
characters.summary: Sir Plume is vain of his amber snuff-box and of the nice conduct of his clouded cane, and has earnest eyes and a round, unthinking face. Sent to demand the lock, he opens his snuff-box and bursts into a string of oaths that ends with an order to give her the hair. In the battle he pulls Clarissa down, is killed by a frown from Chloe, and revives at her smile. He was taken to be Sir George Brown, who, Johnson reports, complained bitterly that he had been made to talk nonsense.
characters.clue: Vain of an amber snuff-box and a clouded cane, he swears his way through a demand for the return of the hair.

characters.name: The Queen of Spleen
characters.role: Goddess of melancholy and ill humour
characters.summary: The goddess of low spirits and the vapours, who lies sighing on her bed in a grotto where only the east wind blows, with Pain at her side and Megrim, or headache, at her head. Umbriel hails her as the ruler of women from fifteen to fifty and the parent of vapours and of female wit. She seems to reject his prayer, but grants it, filling a bag and a vial with the passions and tears he pours on Belinda. The spleen was a fashionable complaint in Pope’s day, called in The Spectator the distemper of the great and the polite.
characters.clue: She sighs for ever in a gloomy grotto between Pain and Megrim, and grants a gnome a bag of sighs and a vial of tears.

characters.name: The speaker
characters.role: The young poet who addresses critics in the Essay
characters.summary: The voice of the Essay belongs to a young poet advising would-be critics: confident, epigrammatic and ready to mock fools, but careful to present himself as modest, the last and meanest of the ancients’ sons, who glows while he reads and trembles as he writes. At the close he honours his dead friend William Walsh and describes his own Muse as not free from faults, nor too vain to mend them. The Essay first appeared without Pope’s name.
characters.clue: He glows while he reads and trembles as he writes, and ends by mourning the friend who taught his Muse to sing.

characters.name: Homer
characters.role: The model poet of the Essay
characters.summary: Homer, the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey, is the Essay’s standard of excellence. Critics are told to read him by day and meditate on him by night, Virgil finds that Nature and Homer are the same, and Aristotle steers by the light of the Maeonian star. When Homer seems to nod, Pope suggests, it is the reader who is dreaming. The Rape of the Lock borrows his gods, his battles, his golden scales and his heroes’ speeches.
characters.clue: Critics are told to read him by day and meditate on him by night, and when he seems to nod it is the reader who dreams.

characters.name: Virgil
characters.role: The Roman poet who imitated Homer
characters.summary: Called young Maro in the Essay, from his full name, Publius Vergilius Maro. Pope imagines him planning the Aeneid as if he were above the critic’s law, until he examines every part and finds that Nature and Homer are the same; he then confines his work to rules as strict as Aristotle’s. The Aeneid lies behind many of the Rape’s jokes, from its opening question to the Baron’s half-granted prayer and Umbriel’s sprig of spleenwort.
characters.clue: As young Maro he designs a work to outlast Rome, then finds that Nature and his great Greek predecessor are the same.

characters.name: Aristotle
characters.role: The first critic, called the Stagirite
characters.summary: Aristotle is called the Stagirite, from his birthplace at Stagira. In the Essay his rules were drawn from the practice of great poets, so that to imitate Homer is to obey them. In Part III he is the first explorer of criticism, who spread his sails and steered by the light of Homer, and poets accepted his laws. Pope also laughs at critics who quote his rules without understanding them, like the Don Quixote of a spurious sequel who reveres Aristotle but will not let a play leave out its combat.
characters.clue: Called the Stagirite, he was the first to leave the shore of criticism, steering by the light of the Maeonian star.

characters.name: William Walsh
characters.summary: Pope’s early adviser was a poet and critic who died in 1708, before the Essay appeared, and whom Pope praises at its close as the Muse’s judge and friend, mild to failings and zealous for merit. Walsh met Pope when he was a teenager and advised him to aim at correctness, which no great English poet had yet achieved. Pope showed him his early work, including a draft of the Essay, and Dryden is said to have called him the best critic in the nation.
characters.clue: Praised at the close as the Muse’s judge and friend, he had taught a young poet to sing and pruned his tender wing.

characters.name: Appius
characters.role: An angry critic, drawn from John Dennis
characters.summary: A critic who reddens at every word you speak and stares, tremendous, like a tyrant in old tapestry. The name came from John Dennis’s tragedy Appius and Virginia (1709), and tremendous was one of Dennis’s favourite words. Dennis answered with an angry pamphlet that attacked Pope’s person as well as his poem, and, as Johnson put it, the hostility between them was never appeased.
characters.clue: He reddens at each word you speak and stares with a threatening eye, like a fierce tyrant in old tapestry.

themes.name: The trivial and the great
themes.summary: The Rape of the Lock names its subject in the second line: mighty contests rising from trivial things. Pope gives a stolen curl the whole apparatus of epic, with gods, prayers, a council, a battle and a transformation, and the joke cuts two ways. The quarrel looks absurd dressed as the Trojan War, and the grand manner looks a little absurd when it fits a card table so well. Now and then something serious appears among the trifles, the hanging of wretches so that jurymen may dine, and the reader sees how badly this society measures what matters.
themes.development: What mighty contests rise from trivial things; When husbands, or when lapdogs breathe their last; the ombre battle; Steel could the labour of the Gods destroy; the lock made a star.

themes.name: Beauty and display
themes.summary: Belinda’s beauty is her power, and Pope describes its making in the language of religion and war: the dressing table is an altar, her reflection a goddess, her cosmetics her arms. Her cross is an ornament. Clarissa states the lesson that beauty fades and good humour must keep what it wins, and the last lines promise that the lock will outlast the head it grew on.
themes.development: The toilet; Puffs, Powders, Patches, Bibles, Billet-doux; the sparkling cross; Fair tresses man’s imperial race ensnare; Clarissa’s speech; the new star.

themes.name: Honour and reputation
themes.summary: Honour in the Rape means reputation, what the town says about a woman. Ariel tells Belinda that the sylphs keep maids safe, though honour is the word with men below. Thalestris fears for Belinda’s name if the Baron shows off the lock, and at Hampton Court a reputation dies at every word. The Baron wants a trophy that will keep his own honour and name alive. Pope’s zeugmas set honour beside brocade, as if the two could be stained in the same way.
themes.development: Tho’ Honour is the word with Men below; stain her honour or her new brocade; At ev’ry word a reputation dies; a degraded toast; the Baron’s boast.

themes.name: Men and women
themes.summary: The poem is a comedy of courtship in which the sexes are at war: belles armed with eyes and fans, beaux who die in metaphor, a baron who plans to win by force or fraud. Its innuendo never stops, from Ariel’s warning to beware of man to Belinda’s wish that the Baron had seized hairs less in sight. Some readers find an affectionate portrait of women in it; others, starting from the dedication’s remarks about the fair sex, find condescension, and note that the moral is spoken by the woman who lent the Baron her scissors.
themes.development: Beware of all, but most beware of Man!; the Baron’s altar; An earthly Lover lurking at her heart; the Cave of Spleen; Hairs less in sight; Clarissa’s speech; the battle of the beaux and belles.

themes.name: Fashion and luxury
themes.summary: Queen Anne’s London is present in every canto: the court at Hampton, the queen taking counsel and tea, gossip, snuff, coffee, china, Indian screens, sedan chairs, patch-boxes and the card game of ombre. The treasures on Belinda’s dressing table come from India and Arabia, with combs of tortoiseshell and ivory, and the fashionable world is seen to depend on trade with half the globe. Pope makes these things glitter, and the glitter is part of the satire.
themes.development: Here thou, great Anna!; This casket India’s glowing gems unlocks; coffee and china; ombre; Where none learn Ombre, none e’er taste Bohea!

themes.name: Nature and the rules
themes.summary: For Pope, Nature is the clear, unchanging, universal order of things that reason recognises, and the rules of poetry are Nature methodised: principles the ancient critics discovered in the practice of the great poets. Following Nature therefore means following the ancients, as Virgil found. Pope also allows a grace beyond the reach of art, a licence that great poets may take when it serves the purpose the rules exist for.
themes.development: First follow Nature; Nature methodiz’d; Nature and Homer were, he found, the same; a grace beyond the reach of art; True Wit is Nature to advantage dress’d.

themes.name: Wit and judgement
themes.summary: Wit in Pope’s time could mean intelligence, invention, a clever turn of phrase or a clever man about town, and the Essay uses the word in several of these senses. Its argument is that wit needs judgement, as a spirited horse needs a rider, and that true wit expresses what oft was thought, but ne’er so well. Dennis complained that the word changes its meaning within a single couplet, and Johnson agreed with him. In the Rape the wits are the beaux, and their wits are weighed against a lady’s hair and found lighter.
themes.development: For wit and judgment often are at strife; True Wit is Nature to advantage dress’d; Some have at first for Wits, then Poets past; the wits mount up, the hairs subside.

themes.name: Pride
themes.summary: Pride is the first cause of bad judgement in the Essay, the never-failing voice of fools, filling up the void where sense is wanting. The good critic is modest, owns his errors and admires superior sense. In the Rape pride is a religion: Belinda’s toilet is the sacred rite of Pride, the Baron boasts that his fame will last for ever, and every character is vain of something, down to Sir Plume and his snuff-box.
themes.development: Is Pride, the never-failing voice of fools; A little learning is a dang’rous thing; the sacred rites of Pride; the Baron’s boast; Sir Plume of amber snuff-box justly vain.

themes.name: Ancients and moderns
themes.summary: Pope wrote during a long argument over whether modern writers could equal the Greeks and Romans, and the Essay mentions critics who prize only the ancients or only the moderns. It takes the side of the ancients: Homer is the model, the rules are theirs, and modern poets may take only the licences the ancients took. It closes with a history in which criticism falls with Rome and revives with Erasmus, Vida and Boileau. The Rape of the Lock sets the ancients’ epic down at a modern tea-table.
themes.development: Be Homer’s works your study and delight; Nature and Homer were, he found, the same; The Ancients only, or the Moderns prize; the history of criticism from Aristotle to Walsh; the machinery of the Rape.

themes.name: The good critic
themes.summary: An Essay on Criticism cares as much about the critic’s character as about poetry. A good critic judges the whole work in the spirit in which it was written, reads without malice, forgives small faults and keeps severity for real vices. He must be candid, modest and well-bred, able to show a friend his faults and to praise a foe. Pope sums up the ideal in the man who is still pleased to teach, and yet not proud to know.
themes.development: A perfect Judge will read each work of Wit / With the same spirit that its author writ; To err is human, to forgive, divine; Men must be taught as if you taught them not; Appius; the portrait of the good critic.

techniques.name: Mock-heroic
techniques.definition: Telling a trivial story in the grand style, with the conventions of epic, so that the mismatch is comic.
techniques.inThisBook: Pope called the Rape an heroi-comical poem, and it uses nearly every convention of epic: a statement of the subject and an invocation, an arming (the toilet), a sacrifice (the Baron’s altar), supernatural guardians, a council of spirits, a formal contest fought as a battle, a descent to the underworld, a hero’s speech, a general battle, divine scales and a final transformation. The distance between the grand form and the small occasion makes the comedy.

techniques.name: Epic machinery
techniques.definition: The gods, angels or spirits who take part in the action of an epic, called its machinery by the critics of Pope’s day.
techniques.inThisBook: None appears in the first version of 1712. For 1714 Pope added the sylphs and gnomes, taking them from Le Comte de Gabalis, a French satire on Rosicrucian ideas about spirits of the elements, and explained the term in his dedication. The sylphs are the souls of dead coquettes, and their duties, guarding fans, powder and petticoats, are the work of epic gods shrunk to the size of a lady’s dressing room. Pope thought that fitting the new machinery to what he had already published was one of his greatest proofs of judgement.

techniques.name: The heroic couplet
techniques.definition: Rhyming pairs of ten-syllable lines, usually closed, so that each pair completes a thought.
techniques.inThisBook: Both poems are in heroic couplets, with an occasional triplet. Pope usually closes the sense at the end of each pair and divides the line at a pause, so that the halves can balance or collide. The Essay praises Denham’s strength and Waller’s sweetness, the poets who made the closed couplet fashionable, and shows how much the form can hold: an argument, a portrait, a joke or a proverb in twenty syllables.

techniques.name: Zeugma
techniques.definition: One verb or phrase governing two words in different senses, often one serious and one trivial.
techniques.inThisBook: Zeugma is the Rape’s favourite comic device: to stain her honour or her new brocade, to lose her heart or necklace at a ball, to take counsel and sometimes tea. The grammar treats the two objects as equal, and the reader has to decide whether the characters do too.

techniques.name: Bathos
techniques.definition: A sudden drop from the lofty to the ridiculous.
techniques.inThisBook: Lists that sink as they go are one of the Rape’s habits: puffs, powders, patches, Bibles, billet-doux; husbands or lapdogs; the towers of Troy and a curl of hair. Pope later made the word the title of a prose satire on bad poets, the Bathos, published in 1728.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Opposed ideas set against each other in balanced phrases.
techniques.inThisBook: The closed couplet invites balance, and Pope uses it to weigh one thing against another: charms strike the sight, but merit wins the soul; to err is human, to forgive, divine; still pleased to praise, yet not afraid to blame. In the Essay the balance expresses judgement itself, faults weighed against merits.

techniques.name: Epic simile
techniques.definition: An extended comparison that develops its second term at length.
techniques.inThisBook: Epic similes are parodied in the Rape, which compares the battle of the beaux and belles to Homer’s gods at war and a dying beau to Ovid’s swan, singing its death-song on the banks of the Maeander. The Essay’s best-known simile is serious: a young scholar climbing the Alps of learning sees hills peep over hills, and Alps on Alps arise.

techniques.name: Allusion
techniques.definition: A passing reference to another text, person or event that the reader is expected to recognise.
techniques.inThisBook: Pope assumes a reader who knows Homer, Virgil and Milton. Clarissa’s speech parodies Sarpedon’s in the Iliad, Jove’s scales come from Homer, Belinda’s bodkin has a pedigree like Agamemnon’s sceptre, Umbriel’s spleenwort recalls the golden bough, and the lock rises to the stars like the lock of Queen Berenice. The Essay alludes to Horace’s nodding Homer, Virgil’s swift Camilla and Dryden’s Alexander’s Feast.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A short balanced sentence that sounds like settled wisdom and usually turns a received idea inside out.
techniques.inThisBook: Many lines of the Essay have become proverbs: a little learning is a dangerous thing; to err is human, to forgive, divine; fools rush in where angels fear to tread. Pope compresses a general truth into a line or a couplet, which is why De Quincey could dismiss the poem as a string of maxims and why readers remember it in pieces.

techniques.name: Sound echoing sense
techniques.definition: Making the sound and movement of a line imitate what it describes.
techniques.inThisBook: In the passage on versification in the Essay, Pope performs what he describes: ten low words creep in one dull line, a needless Alexandrine drags its slow length along, the line labours when Ajax heaves a rock, and a line of twelve syllables skims along the main with swift Camilla. The Rape puts the same skill to comic use: fans clap, silks rustle, and tough whalebones crack.

techniques.name: Innuendo
techniques.definition: A suggestion, usually sexual, left for the reader to catch.
techniques.inThisBook: The Rape is full of double meanings, beginning with its title, in which rape still meant a seizure or theft. The nymph may break Diana’s law, beaux die in metaphor, and Belinda wishes the Baron had seized hairs less in sight. Pope never states the second meaning, which is how the poem stays polite.

quotations.text: What dire offence from am'rous causes springs, / What mighty contests rise from trivial things,
quotations.context: The first lines of the poem, before Pope names his friend Caryll and calls on the Muse.
quotations.analysis: Epic poems begin by announcing their subject, as the Iliad announces the anger of Achilles. Pope announces a quarrel from amorous causes, and his second line admits that the contest is mighty only in its effects. The rhyme of springs and things sets the scale of the whole poem.

quotations.text: 'Tis but their Sylph, the wise Celestials know, / Tho' Honour is the word with Men below.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: In Belinda’s dream, Ariel explains what keeps maids safe at balls and midnight masquerades.
quotations.analysis: According to Ariel, maids stay chaste because sylphs guard them, whatever men may call it. Honour becomes a word for public use, while the real safeguard is invisible and a little absurd. The couplet is an early sign that the poem treats virtue as a matter of what can be seen.

quotations.text: Beware of all, but most beware of Man!
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: The last line of Ariel’s warning, after he admits that heaven has not shown him what the danger is.
quotations.analysis: Ariel foresees a dreadful event but not its shape, so his warning covers every man Belinda will meet. It sounds like an oracle and works as a joke about chaperones. Belinda forgets it as soon as she wakes to a love letter.

quotations.text: This casket India's glowing gems unlocks, / And all Arabia breathes from yonder box.
quotations.context: At the dressing table the various offerings of the world are laid out for Belinda.
quotations.analysis: Jewels from India and perfume from Arabia arrive at the dressing table as offerings to a goddess. Pope enjoys the richness of the list, and he also shows that a London lady’s morning depends on the trade of half the world. The next couplet adds combs of tortoiseshell and ivory.

quotations.text: Here files of pins extend their shining rows, / Puffs, Powders, Patches, Bibles, Billet-doux.
quotations.context: The list of things on Belinda’s dressing table ends here, just before Beauty puts on all its arms.
quotations.analysis: Pins stand in files like soldiers, and every item in the second line begins with P or B, so that Bibles become one more cosmetic among puffs and patches. Love letters lie beside scripture with no sense of difference. It is one of the best-known lines of bathos in English.

quotations.text: On her white breast a sparkling Cross she wore, / Which Jews might kiss, and Infidels adore.
quotations.context: Belinda sails up the Thames, and every eye is fixed on her.
quotations.analysis: Belinda’s cross is jewellery, admired even by those who reject what it stands for. Pope balances kiss and adore so neatly that the religious sign disappears into its effect on the onlookers. Her faith, like the Bibles on her table, is part of the display.

quotations.text: But chiefly Love—to Love an Altar built, / Of twelve vast French Romances, neatly gilt.
quotations.context: Before dawn the Baron prays to every power for the lock, and to Love above all.
quotations.analysis: Heroes in epic sacrifice to the gods before battle, and the Baron builds his altar from French romances, the enormous gilt-bound love stories of fashionable reading. He burns the trophies of his former loves on it. The gods grant half his prayer, as Apollo grants half of a warrior’s prayer in the Aeneid: he will win the lock but not keep it.

quotations.text: Or some frail China jar receive a flaw; / Or stain her honour or her new brocade; / Forget her pray'rs, or miss a masquerade; / Or lose her heart, or necklace, at a ball;
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Ariel tells the sylphs that black omens threaten Belinda, though he cannot tell whether the nymph shall break Diana’s law or suffer something smaller.
quotations.analysis: Each line sets a serious loss beside a trivial one: honour beside brocade, prayers beside a masquerade, a heart beside a necklace. The zeugma makes it impossible to say which Ariel fears more, and perhaps which Belinda would. Collecting china was a new fashion, brought over from Holland by Queen Mary.

quotations.text: Here thou, great Anna! whom three realms obey, / Dost sometimes counsel take—and sometimes Tea.
quotations.context: Hampton Court is introduced as the palace where statesmen meet and the queen sometimes stays.
quotations.analysis: Queen Anne receives full ceremony until the last word. The dash before Tea makes the reader wait, and the zeugma sets affairs of state beside a luxury that in 1710 cost from twelve to twenty-eight shillings a pound. Politics and pleasure share one verb.

quotations.text: The hungry Judges soon the sentence sign, / And wretches hang that jury-men may dine;
quotations.context: As the afternoon wears on at Hampton Court, the poem glances at the law courts.
quotations.analysis: Here hungry judges hurry their sentences, and men are hanged so that the jury can get to dinner. The couplet keeps the balance of the rest of the canto, but its subject is death, and it shows what happens to people outside the fashionable world when their lives are weighed against a meal.

quotations.text: Let Spades be trumps! she said, and trumps they were.
quotations.context: Belinda reviews her cards at ombre and declares trumps.
quotations.analysis: God said, Let there be light: and there was light. The line gives Belinda’s declaration the same creative power. In ombre the player who names trumps becomes the ombre and plays alone against the other two, so for a moment her word is law.

quotations.text: Sudden he view'd, in spite of all her art, / An earthly Lover lurking at her heart.
quotations.context: Just before the Baron closes the scissors, Ariel looks into Belinda’s thoughts.
quotations.analysis: Sylphs can protect only women who reject mankind, and Ariel finds a lover hidden in Belinda’s heart. Pope never says who it is. The discovery hints that Belinda is less indifferent to men than she seems, and Ariel, amazed and confused, finds his power gone and retires with a sigh.

quotations.text: Not louder shrieks to pitying heav'n are cast, / When husbands, or when lapdogs breathe their last;
quotations.context: The lock is cut, and Belinda screams.
quotations.analysis: Belinda’s screams are compared to the shrieks of ladies at the death of husbands or of lapdogs, and the line places the two side by side as if they were equal losses. The next couplet adds broken china. It is the poem’s sharpest line on a society that cannot tell great things from small.

quotations.text: While nymphs take treats, or assignations give, / So long my honour, name, and praise shall live!
quotations.speaker: The Baron
quotations.context: The victor claims his prize, beginning Let wreaths of triumph now my temples twine.
quotations.analysis: Epic heroes are promised glory as long as rivers run and stars shine. The Baron measures his fame by the social calendar instead: visits, wax-lights, treats and assignations. His boast is funny because everything he names lasts exactly as long as the fashions of one season.

quotations.text: Hail, wayward Queen! / Who rule the sex to fifty from fifteen: / Parent of vapours and of female wit, / Who give th' hysteric, or poetic fit,
quotations.speaker: Umbriel
quotations.context: In the Cave of Spleen, Umbriel addresses the goddess.
quotations.analysis: Umbriel flatters the goddess as the ruler of women’s moods from fifteen to fifty. Vapours were a fashionable form of low spirits thought to afflict women in particular, and Pope makes spleen the source of illness and bad writing alike: she makes some take physic, others scribble plays. The joke falls on women writers as well as on fashionable invalids.

quotations.text: Methinks already I your tears survey, / Already hear the horrid things they say, / Already see you a degraded toast, / And all your honour in a whisper lost!
quotations.speaker: Thalestris
quotations.context: Thalestris rouses Belinda to revenge.
quotations.analysis: Thalestris fears only what people will say: the tears, the horrid talk, and Belinda fallen from her place as a toast, a beauty whose health is drunk by admirers. The repeated already hurries the disaster forward. Honour, in her account, is something lost in a whisper.

quotations.text: My Lord, why, what the devil? / Z—ds! damn the lock! 'fore Gad, you must be civil!
quotations.speaker: Sir Plume
quotations.context: Sent by Thalestris to demand the lock, Sir Plume opens his snuff-box and speaks.
quotations.analysis: An epic hero would deliver a formal challenge. Sir Plume manages a string of oaths, one of them printed with a dash, and a demand that the Baron be civil. Pope’s joke is that he has nothing to say, and Sir George Brown, who was taken to be the original, was angry about it for a long time.

quotations.text: Hairs less in sight, or any hairs but these!
quotations.speaker: Belinda
quotations.context: The last line of Belinda’s lament, which begins Oh hadst thou, cruel! been content to seize.
quotations.analysis: Belinda means that she wishes the Baron had taken a lock from somewhere less visible, and the double meaning is left to the reader. Her concern is still for what can be seen. Readers have long argued over whether Pope is laughing at her innocence or hinting that she is less innocent than she seems.

quotations.text: Since painted, or not painted, all shall fade, / And she who scorns a man, must die a maid; / What then remains but well our pow'r to use, / And keep good-humour still whate'er we lose?
quotations.speaker: Clarissa
quotations.context: Clarissa’s speech, added in 1717, asks why beauties are praised and honoured most.
quotations.analysis: Clarissa’s argument is practical. Painted or not, every face will fade, and a woman who scorns men will die unmarried, so she should use her power well and keep her temper. The speech parodies Sarpedon’s in the Iliad, where a hero argues that since men must die they should win glory; Clarissa’s glory is good humour. Belinda frowns, and Thalestris calls her a prude.

quotations.text: All side in parties, and begin th' attack; / Fans clap, silks rustle, and tough whalebones crack;
quotations.context: Thalestris cries To arms, to arms!, and the battle begins.
quotations.analysis: Fashion supplies the weapons: fans, silk dresses and the whalebone stays inside them. The second line claps, rustles and cracks like the things it names, one blunt word after another. Homer’s battles ring with bronze; this one sounds like a crowded drawing room.

quotations.text: Now Jove suspends his golden scales in air, / Weighs the Men's wits against the Lady's hair; / The doubtful beam long nods from side to side; / At length the wits mount up, the hairs subside.
quotations.context: In the middle of the battle, the poem turns to the gods.
quotations.analysis: In the Iliad Zeus weighs the fates of armies in golden scales, and Milton borrowed the image for Paradise Lost. Here the pans hold the men’s wits and a lady’s hair. The wits rise because they are lighter, a verdict on the beaux and on the whole quarrel.

quotations.text: "Restore the Lock!" she cries; and all around / "Restore the Lock!" the vaulted roofs rebound.
quotations.context: Belinda has thrown snuff at the Baron and drawn her bodkin, whose pedigree parodies that of Agamemnon’s sceptre.
quotations.analysis: Belinda’s demand is repeated by the vaulted roofs of Hampton Court like a battle cry in an epic hall. Pope then compares her to Othello roaring for the handkerchief, another small object carrying the weight of honour and jealousy. By now the lock has disappeared.

quotations.text: When those fair suns shall set, as set they must, / And all those tresses shall be laid in dust, / This Lock, the Muse shall consecrate to fame, / And 'midst the stars inscribe Belinda's name.
quotations.context: The last lines of the poem, addressed to Belinda.
quotations.analysis: Pope ends with a compliment that is also a claim for poetry. Belinda’s eyes, the fair suns, will set and her hair will be laid in dust, but the Muse will fix the lock among the stars, as the lock of Queen Berenice was said to have become a constellation. The promise has come true: Arabella Fermor is remembered because of the poem.

quotations.text: 'Tis with our judgments as our watches, none / Go just alike, yet each believes his own.
quotations.context: Early in Part I, on why critics disagree.
quotations.analysis: Judgements are compared to watches: no two keep the same time, and each owner believes his own. The comparison is homely and exact, and the line break after none makes the reader wait for the verb. It introduces the Essay’s concern with knowing the limits of one’s own taste.

quotations.text: First follow Nature, and your judgment frame / By her just standard, which is still the same:
quotations.context: The central instruction of Part I, after the warning to know the limits of one’s own wit.
quotations.analysis: Nature here means the order of things as reason understands it, universal and unchanging, the same for every age. Pope makes it a standard, a measure against which judgement is framed. The next lines call Nature the source, the end and the test of art.

quotations.text: Those Rules of old discovered, not devis'd, / Are Nature still, but Nature methodiz'd;
quotations.context: Pope explains where the rules of poetry come from.
quotations.analysis: Rules were discovered in the practice of the great poets, and critics only set them in order, so obeying them is obeying Nature. The antithesis of discovered and devised carries the argument. The next couplet compares Nature to liberty, restrained only by the laws it made itself.

quotations.text: But when t' examine ev'ry part he came, / Nature and Homer were, he found, the same.
quotations.context: Pope imagines young Virgil planning the Aeneid and scorning to draw from anything but Nature’s fountains.
quotations.analysis: Virgil sets out to draw only from Nature and discovers, on close study, that Homer has done it before him. Imitating the ancients is therefore the same as following Nature. The line packs the neoclassical creed into ten syllables.

quotations.text: From vulgar bounds with brave disorder part, / And snatch a grace beyond the reach of art,
quotations.context: Pope allows that some beauties lie beyond the reach of any rule.
quotations.analysis: Pegasus, the winged horse of poetry, may leave the common track and take a nearer way. Brave disorder is a deliberate paradox, and Pope permits it only where it serves the purpose of the rules. Even this licence belongs chiefly to the ancients; moderns are told to beware.

quotations.text: Of all the Causes which conspire to blind / Man's erring judgment, and misguide the mind, / What the weak head with strongest bias rules, / Is Pride, the never-failing voice of fools.
quotations.context: Part II opens with the causes of bad judgement.
quotations.analysis: Pride comes first among the causes of bad judgement, and it rules the weak head most strongly because such a head has least else to steer by. Pope’s sentence holds its subject back for four lines and delivers it at the end. The following lines say that pride fills up the mighty void of sense.

quotations.text: A little learning is a dang'rous thing;
quotations.context: The second cause of bad criticism. The next line reads Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring.
quotations.analysis: Learning is dangerous in small amounts because it makes a student confident before it makes him wise. The Pierian spring belongs to the Muses, and shallow draughts of it intoxicate while deep drinking sobers. Pope follows the couplet with a young climber in the Alps who sees new peaks rise at every step.

quotations.text: True Wit is Nature to advantage dress'd, / What oft was thought, but ne'er so well express'd;
quotations.context: Pope has been mocking critics who care only for conceits, glittering thoughts struck out at every line, and the poets who supply them.
quotations.analysis: True wit, on this definition, gives a common thought its best expression, so that readers recognise it as true at first sight. Novelty lies in the phrasing. Pope’s couplet proves the point, since the idea was old and his wording made it memorable.

quotations.text: A needless Alexandrine ends the song / That, like a wounded snake, drags its slow length along.
quotations.context: Pope mocks critics who judge a poem only by the smoothness of its metre, and the poets who please them with worn-out rhymes.
quotations.analysis: An Alexandrine is a line of six feet in place of the usual five. Pope makes the second line one, loaded with long syllables and heavy stresses, so that it drags along as it describes. He is making fun of poets who end a paragraph with one out of habit.

quotations.text: 'Tis not enough no harshness gives offence, / The sound must seem an Echo to the sense:
quotations.context: Pope has just praised Denham’s strength and Waller’s sweetness, the masters of the smooth couplet.
quotations.analysis: Avoiding harsh sounds is only the beginning; the sound of verse should imitate its meaning. The following lines demonstrate: a smooth line for the west wind, a rough one for the torrent, a labouring line for Ajax and a skimming one for swift Camilla.

quotations.text: Good-nature and good-sense must ever join; / To err is human, to forgive, divine.
quotations.context: Towards the end of Part II, after lines on the envy and the lust of praise that set writers against each other.
quotations.analysis: Good nature and good sense are joined in the first line, and error and forgiveness are divided between humanity and God in the second. The antithesis gives forgiveness a divine status, and the line has become one of the most quoted in English. In context it is advice to critics tempted to attack other writers out of envy.

quotations.text: And stares, tremendous, with a threat'ning eye, / Like some fierce Tyrant in old tapestry.
quotations.context: Some critics cannot bear to be corrected: But Appius reddens at each word you speak.
quotations.analysis: Appius was John Dennis, author of the tragedy Appius and Virginia, and tremendous was one of his favourite words. The simile shrinks his rage to a figure on a faded wall-hanging. Dennis replied with a pamphlet that mocked Pope’s body as well as his poem.

quotations.text: Nay, fly to Altars; there they'll talk you dead: / For Fools rush in where Angels fear to tread.
quotations.context: Pope describes the bookful blockhead, a critic who talks everywhere, even in St Paul’s.
quotations.analysis: Such critics will talk you dead even at the altar, where a fugitive might hope for sanctuary. The second line has become a proverb, but in the Essay it describes a particular kind of critic, one with loads of learned lumber in his head and no sense of where he is.

quotations.text: Careless of censure, nor too fond of fame; / Still pleas'd to praise, yet not afraid to blame, / Averse alike to flatter, or offend; / Not free from faults, nor yet too vain to mend.
quotations.context: The last lines of the Essay, describing the poet’s own Muse after the death of Walsh.
quotations.analysis: Ending on a self-portrait, the Essay follows its own advice: balanced, modest and fair. Each line holds two opposite faults in check. After so many attacks on other critics, it is a disarming final move.

timeline.label: Alexander Pope is born
timeline.detail: On 21 May, in Lombard Street, London, the son of a Catholic linen draper.

timeline.label: Binfield
timeline.detail: By this year the family has moved to Binfield in Windsor Forest; as Catholics they are barred from many schools and offices, and Pope largely educates himself.

timeline.label: William Walsh
timeline.detail: The critic William Walsh befriends the young poet and advises him to aim at correctness.

timeline.label: The Pastorals
timeline.detail: Pope’s Pastorals appear in Tonson’s Poetical Miscellanies. In his collected works he later dated An Essay on Criticism to this year.

timeline.label: An Essay on Criticism
timeline.detail: Published without Pope’s name on 15 May. John Dennis replies with an angry pamphlet, and on 20 December Addison praises the Essay in The Spectator.

timeline.label: The lock is cut
timeline.detail: Robert, Lord Petre, cuts a lock of Arabella Fermor’s hair, and a friend of both families asks Pope for a poem to end the quarrel.

timeline.label: The first Rape of the Lock
timeline.detail: A version in two cantos appears without Pope’s name in Lintot’s Miscellany in May.

timeline.label: Five cantos
timeline.detail: The enlarged Rape of the Lock is published separately, with the sylphs and gnomes and a dedication to Arabella Fermor.

timeline.label: The Iliad
timeline.detail: The first volume of Pope’s translation appears; by the last volume in 1720 the subscriptions have made him independent for life.

timeline.label: Clarissa’s speech
timeline.detail: Pope adds Clarissa’s speech to the Rape in his collected Works. His father dies in October.

timeline.label: Twickenham
timeline.detail: Pope takes the lease of a house with five acres beside the Thames at Twickenham, where he lives for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: The Dunciad
timeline.detail: Pope’s mock-epic on dull writers appears in May, after the Bathos, his prose satire on bad poets.

timeline.label: Pope dies
timeline.detail: On 30 May at Twickenham, where he is buried near his parents.

timeline.label: Warburton’s edition
timeline.detail: William Warburton publishes Pope’s Works in nine volumes, with his last corrections and a long commentary on the Essay.

places.name: Hampton Court Palace
places.note: The palace on the Thames, begun by Wolsey and enlarged by William III, where the Rape’s game of ombre and the cutting of the lock take place.

places.name: Lombard Street, London
places.note: Where Pope was born in 1688; his father had moved his linen business there.

places.name: Binfield, Windsor Forest
places.note: The village where Pope grew up and wrote his early poems, including An Essay on Criticism.

places.name: Twickenham
places.note: Pope’s home from 1719 until his death; he is buried in the parish church.

places.name: St James’s Park and the Mall
places.note: Where the beau monde strolled, and where the Rape says the new star will be hailed with music.

criticalViews.summary: Johnson thought the Rape the lightest, most inventive and most enjoyable of all Pope’s poems, and many readers since have admired how completely its epic machinery is fitted to the action. Pope himself thought the recasting of 1714 one of his greatest proofs of judgement. On this view the poem’s form is close to perfect and its satire is light and good-humoured.
criticalViews.counter: The lightness has been questioned. The poem’s picture of society includes hanged wretches and a trade that reaches round the world, and its jokes about women can be read as contempt dressed as gallantry.

criticalViews.position: Satire of women or of society
criticalViews.summary: Feminist critics have read the Rape as a poem about how a woman is displayed, judged and possessed, in which the assault on Belinda is laughed off and the moral is spoken by the woman who handed over the scissors. Others read it as a satire on the whole fashionable world, men as much as women, with the Baron, Sir Plume and the beaux as absurd as any belle.
criticalViews.counter: Pope said the poem was meant to divert young ladies with good sense and good humour enough to laugh at their own follies, and Arabella Fermor, by Johnson’s account, liked it well enough to show it to her friends, although her family later resented it.

criticalViews.position: The Essay as a creed of its age
criticalViews.summary: Parrott, like many readers after the Romantics, treated the Essay as a statement of the accepted ideas of its time, polished but hardly original, and De Quincey dismissed it as a string of maxims. Its value, on this view, lies in its expression.
criticalViews.counter: Johnson thought the Essay showed a range of learning and judgement rarely reached even in old age, and its three-part argument, with its demand for humane and candid criticism, is more coherent than the maxims suggest.

essayQuestions.question: How does Pope use the conventions of epic in The Rape of the Lock, and to what effect?
plan: Begin with the statement of the subject and the invocation: mighty contests from trivial things.
Analyse the toilet as an arming scene and the Baron’s altar as a sacrifice.
Examine the sylphs as epic machinery, and the ombre game as a battle.
Discuss the Cave of Spleen as a descent to the underworld and Clarissa’s speech as a heroic speech.
Conclude on whether the mock-epic diminishes the characters, the epic, or both.

essayQuestions.question: How does The Rape of the Lock present women and the relations between the sexes?
essayQuestions.focus: Belinda, Clarissa, Thalestris and the beaux
plan: Consider the dedication to Arabella Fermor and its account of the poem’s purpose.
Analyse Belinda at her dressing table and at ombre: beauty as power.
Examine the innuendo of the lock, the petticoat and Belinda’s lament.
Weigh Clarissa’s speech against the reactions of Belinda and Thalestris.
Evaluate whether the poem mocks women, society, or its own epic machinery.

essayQuestions.question: What, according to An Essay on Criticism, makes a good critic?
essayQuestions.focus: Nature, the ancients, pride and manners
plan: Explain what Pope means by following Nature and by Nature methodised.
Discuss the role of the ancients, with Virgil and Homer.
Analyse the causes of bad judgement in Part II: pride, a little learning, partiality.
Examine the portrait of the good critic and the history of criticism in Part III.
Assess how far Pope’s own couplets practise what the Essay preaches.

discussionQuestions: Why might Pope have added the sylphs and gnomes to a poem that had already succeeded without them?
Is Belinda a heroine, a victim or a target of the satire?
What does Clarissa’s speech add to the poem, and why does no one applaud it?
Which lines of An Essay on Criticism have become proverbs, and does their meaning change out of context?
Can Pope’s idea of following Nature still guide a reader or critic today?
How do the two poems throw light on each other?

related.why: Homer’s war, which the Rape parodies from Clarissa’s speech to Jove’s golden scales, and which Pope translated between 1715 and 1720.
Virgil’s epic, the model for the Rape’s invocation and prayers and, in the Essay, the proof that Nature and Homer were the same.
Milton’s angels and golden scales, which the sylphs and the battle of the beaux gently mock.
Satire by Pope’s friend and fellow member of the Scriblerus Club, Jonathan Swift.
